title: Senior's toolkit: branches, merges and rebases
summary: Fixup commits, autosquash, rebase --onto, stacked branches, rerere and conflict tools.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: branches, merges and rebases
steps.body: These keep a pull request clean while it is reviewed, and take the pain out of conflicts you have already solved once.

toolkit.what: Records a small fix that belongs to an earlier commit in your branch. The rebase below folds it in for you.
toolkit.when: a reviewer asks for a change to commit 2 of 5

toolkit.what: Opens the todo list with every `fixup!` commit already moved under its target. Save, and the history is clean.
flags: config to make it the default

toolkit.what: Moves only the commits after `oldbase` onto `newbase`. Fixes a branch built on another branch that was squash-merged or rewritten.
flags: where the commits should end up
the last commit you do NOT want to move

toolkit.what: When you rebase the top of a stack of branches, also moves every branch inside the stack. Stacked pull requests stay in step.
flags: update branches that point into the rewritten commits
toolkit.when: you keep several small dependent PRs

toolkit.what: Git records how you resolved a conflict and replays the same resolution next time the same conflict appears.
flags: drop a resolution you got wrong
toolkit.when: long-lived branches that are rebased again and again

toolkit.what: During a conflict, take one side for a whole file. In a merge, ours is your branch; in a rebase they are swapped: ours is the base you rebase onto.
flags: merge: your branch; rebase: the upstream
merge: the other branch; rebase: your commit being replayed
toolkit.example: git checkout --theirs package-lock.json && git add package-lock.json

toolkit.what: Conflict markers also show the common ancestor, so you can see what each side changed instead of guessing.
flags: three-way markers with the shared lines moved out
go back to before the operation

toolkit.what: Copies one commit onto the current branch, for example a fix from main onto a release branch.
flags: append `(cherry picked from commit ...)` so the trail is visible

steps.prompt: Match each command to the situation it is for.
pairs: a review fix that belongs in an earlier commit
keep a stack of dependent branches in step
the same conflict keeps coming back
backport one fix to a release branch

steps.prompt: Fold a review fix into commit `a1b2c3d` of your branch.
steps.explain: `--fixup` makes a `fixup! ...` commit; `--autosquash` moves it under its target in the todo list. `--amend` only changes the latest commit, not commit 2 of 5.

steps.prompt: You run `git rebase origin/main` and get a conflict in `Program.cs`. You want to keep the version from your own commit. You ran `git checkout --ours Program.cs` and got main's version instead. Why?
options: During a rebase the sides are swapped: `--ours` is the branch you rebase onto, so you need `--theirs`
steps.explain: A rebase replays your commits on top of the upstream, so HEAD (ours) is the upstream and the commit being applied (theirs) is yours. Run `git checkout --theirs Program.cs`, `git add` it and `git rebase --continue`.

steps.prompt: `feature/b` was branched from `feature/a`. `feature/a` was squash-merged into main. Now `git rebase origin/main` on `feature/b` replays all of a's old commits and conflicts on every one. What should you run?
steps.explain: The squash commit on main has a different id from a's commits, so Git thinks they are new. `--onto` says: take only the commits after `feature/a` and put them on main.

steps.prompt: A reviewer asked for a change to an earlier commit. Put the workflow in order.
Which commands rewrite existing commits, and which only add new ones?

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Turn on `rerere` and `zdiff3` on day one; they cost nothing. While a PR is in review, answer comments with `--fixup` commits and squash them with `--autosquash` just before merge, so reviewers can see what changed and the final history stays clean.
